title: A Carriage from the Junk Heap

banner.alt: A rough two-wheeled carriage with a horse on a dirt road at dusk, the North Star above, and a train waiting in the distance

keepsake.name: quilt square
keepsake.line: Only Imagination Trip travelers earn this one. Pieced from scraps, like the quilt Old Rit sewed.

postcard.h: Two wheels and two stout boards
body: Ben is in the one-room jail, and Harriet’s parents are past eighty. They could never walk north. So the children search the junk heap.
Build what she made from it.
postcard.word: A chaise is a light two-wheeled carriage. Harriet’s wheels came from an old one.

mission.p: Put the carriage from Chapter 12 together, part by part, with the horse in front.

steps.build:
Open your menu (top button, right controller) and click Models. Build in this order:
  1. two wheels, the same size
  2. a board between them for the seat, one below for the footrest
  3. rope to hang the footrest
  4. the horse in front, the quilt on the seat

steps.frame: “The ___ ___ for the old folks. In Chapter 12, ___.”
steps.extra: Put the Western Town Green Train down the road with a Lantern On: the steam cars at Burrsville.
steps.fits: the horse and the whole carriage

points: Your video is 30 seconds or less, shows the wheels, boards, rope, horse and quilt, and you say 2 sentences: one part of the rescue and what it did for the old folks, with a detail from Chapter 12.

alt.p: Chapters 11 and 12 are full of messages that mean more than they say. Match each one to its real meaning.

pairs.a: “When the good old ship of Zion comes along, be ready to step on board.”
pairs.b: Harriet is coming. Brothers, be ready.

pairs.a: Two live chickens let loose in the street
pairs.b: a trick so John Stewart would not see her face
pairs.why: He laughs at the little old woman chasing her birds and never looks twice.

pairs.a: A sunbonnet and a dusty shawl
pairs.b: Harriet’s disguise as an elderly granny
pairs.why: On every trip she dresses as a man or an old woman.

pairs.b: Harriet has arrived to rescue Ben
pairs.why: Old Rit sings it when she brings his breakfast to the jail. Ben’s eyes light up.

pairs.b: be ready tonight, when they come
pairs.why: The second song, sung as the key grates in the lock.

pairs.a: A handkerchief tied over Ben’s eyes
pairs.b: so Ben can honestly say he never saw his children

alt.miss: Not that one. Ask who sent the signal, and who was supposed to understand it.

write.q: Pick one part of the rescue: a wheel, a board, the rope, the horse, the quilt, the tickets or the lantern. In 2 sentences, say what it did for the old folks, with one detail from Chapter 12.

scripts.brief: Hey, it’s Marcus. In Chapter 12 Old Ben is in a one-room jail, and Harriet’s parents are past eighty. They could never walk north. So she sends the village children to the junk heap for two wheels and two stout boards, and borrows Jacob Jackson’s old horse. Build the carriage she put together, part by part, and tell me what one part did for the old folks.
scripts.alt: No headset? Take the window seat. Chapters 11 and 12 are full of signals: a letter about a ship, two loose chickens, a song at the jail door. Match each one to what it really meant, and you will see how Harriet talked without being understood by the wrong people.
scripts.saved: The carriage is built, and the quilt is over the seat. That quilt and Ben’s broadax were the only things the old folks took from slavery. Here is your square of it. Keep it close.

testPara: The quilt covered the old folks' legs on the narrow seat. In Chapter 12 it mattered because it and Ben's broadax were the only things they took from slavery.
